verdict.rationale: The proposition hangs on the institution linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν) in 'This is my body' (Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου, 1 Corinthians 11:24), and the lexicon itself glosses 'to be' (εἰμί) as the verb to be with various uses and significations, so the bare grammar carries both literal identity and figurative predication (a 'X is Y' statement that is not strict identity) and cannot by itself fix a local bodily presence in, with, and under the elements. The same linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν) links subject to predicate in 'I am the vine' (John 15:1), 'I am the door' (John 10:9), 'I am the bread' (John 6:35), 'the rock was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:4), and 'these are two covenants' (Galatians 4:24), where no substantial co-location is meant. The real-presence-flavored anchors are genuine: 'sharing' or 'participation' (κοινωνία, koinonia) in 1 Corinthians 10:16 makes the cup and bread a sharing in the blood and body of Christ, and 'gnaw' or 'chew' (τρώγω, trogo) in John 6:54-58 is a visceral gnaw or chew verb. But 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) means participation and fellowship, which the words do not narrow to bodily co-presence rather than spiritual or covenantal union, and John 6:63 says the flesh profits nothing and the words are spirit. The phrase 'in, with, and under' is a metaphysical specification (a precise philosophical claim about how something exists) the vocabulary never supplies, so the lexical pattern is materially contested.

scripture.reasoning: 'This is my body' (Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου), sets the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) between the demonstrative 'this' (οὗτος, houtos) pointing at the broken bread and the predicate 'body' (σῶμα, soma). The brief lexicon glosses 'to be' (εἰμί, eimi) as the verb to be with various uses and significations, so the present indicative (an ongoing, simple statement of fact) here is the same form used both for literal identity and for figurative predication (a 'X is Y' statement used as a figure of speech) across the canon, and on its own it neither requires nor excludes a bodily presence in or under the element. The clause closes with 'for my remembrance' (εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν), where 'remembrance' (ἀνάμνησις, anamnesis) means recollection, orienting the act toward calling to mind an absent referent rather than toward a metaphysical change (a change at the deepest level of what something is) or a co-location of body with bread.

The cup word, 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' (τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ αἵματι), predicates the 'cup' (ποτήριον, poterion) as the 'covenant' (διαθήκη, diatheke), not as blood located in or under the liquid. Reading the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) here as strict local identity would make the cup itself the covenant, which the predicate forbids, so the same linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) in the parallel bread word likewise resists a flat localized-presence construal. The repeated 'do this for my remembrance' (τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν, with 'remembrance' = ἀνάμνησις, anamnesis) reinforces a remembrance frame. The phrase 'in my blood' (ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ αἵματι) uses the preposition 'in' (ἐν, en), but 'in' (ἐν, en) here marks the sphere of the covenant in the blood, not a metaphysical 'in, with, and under' (a precise philosophical claim about location) that the wording would have to spell out.

'You proclaim the Lord's death until he comes' (τὸν θάνατον τοῦ κυρίου καταγγέλλετε ἄχρι οὗ ἔλθῃ), sets the rite within an interval bounded by 'until' (ἄχρι, achri), with the aorist subjunctive (a completed-action verb form used in conditional or future-leaning clauses) 'he comes' (ἔλθῃ, from ἔρχομαι, erchomai) of a future coming. The grammar presupposes that the Lord is awaited and not yet arrived bodily, which fits a present bodily absence rather than a continuous bodily presence localized with each loaf ('bread' = ἄρτος, artos) and cup.

'The cup ... is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread ... is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?' (τὸ ποτήριον ... οὐχὶ κοινωνία ἐστὶν τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ; τὸν ἄρτον ... οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;), the 'cup' (ποτήριον, poterion) is a 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) of the blood of Christ and the 'bread' (ἄρτος, artos) a 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) of the 'body' (σῶμα, soma) of Christ. This is the strongest real-presence-flavored anchor, and the verse really does join the elements to the body and blood. But the brief lexicon glosses 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) as participation, and across its eighteen occurrences the word denotes fellowship, sharing, and participation, never substantial co-location (two things sharing the same location at the deepest level of being). The text affirms a real participation in Christ through the elements, yet the vocabulary does not specify whether that participation is by bodily presence in or under the bread, by a substantial change (a change at the deepest level of being), by a spiritual reception, or by covenantal union, so it underdetermines the 'in, with, and under' formula.

'The one who eats my flesh and drinks my blood' (ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ πίνων μου τὸ αἷμα). The verb 'gnaw' or 'chew' (τρώγω, trogo) is glossed as to gnaw, munch, crunch of animals and to eat of men, a more visceral word than the ordinary 'eat' (ἐσθίω, esthio), and it recurs in John 6:54, 56, 57, 58, intensifying the eating language that a bodily-presence reading invokes. This is genuine lexical weight on the realism side. The realism it forces is the realism of true participation in Christ, but the discourse does not itself supply the metaphysics (the deep account of what is really going on at the level of being) of how the 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) is present, so it does not by itself establish a presence in or under bread.

'The Spirit is what gives life, the flesh profits nothing' (τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν τὸ ζῳοποιοῦν, ἡ σὰρξ οὐκ ὠφελεῖ οὐδέν), with 'the words I have spoken to you are spirit and are life' (τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἐγὼ λελάληκα ὑμῖν πνεῦμά ἐστιν καὶ ζωή ἐστιν, where 'is' = ἐστιν, estin, from 'to be' = εἰμί, eimi). Coming at the close of the same bread discourse that used 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo), this dominical (spoken by the Lord himself) comment relativizes a crassly fleshly eating and steers reception toward a spiritual mode. The referent of 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) in this verse is itself contested, whether it denies a fleshly eating of the bread or names a broader carnal mode of understanding, so the verse counterweights the visceral 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo) without settling the mode.

'See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself, handle me and see' (ἴδετε τὰς χεῖράς μου καὶ τοὺς πόδας μου ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι αὐτός, ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε, with 'I am' from 'to be' = εἰμί, eimi), with 'a spirit does not have flesh and bones' (πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει). The verb 'touch' or 'handle' (ψηλαφάω, pselaphao) is to touch or handle, and 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) with 'bone' (ὀστέον, osteon) presents the risen body as touchable and locally bounded, seen and handled in one place. A single body so described is in tension with the same body being bodily present with bread in many places at once.

'He was lifted up and a cloud took him from their eyes' (ἐπήρθη καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν, with 'him' = αὐτός, autos). The verb 'lift up' (ἐπαίρω, epairo) is to lift up and the prepositional phrase 'from the eyes' (ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν) marks spatial removal, so the same body just seen is narrated as departing upward and away, framing his post-ascension presence as bodily located in 'heaven' (οὐρανός, ouranos) rather than diffused under earthly elements.

'This same Jesus who was taken up from you into heaven will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven' (οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὁ ἀναλημφθεὶς ἀφ' ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε αὐτὸν πορευόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The demonstrative 'this' (οὗτος, houtos) ties the future bodily return to the very body taken up by 'take up' (ἀναλαμβάνω, analambano), and the future 'he will come' (ἐλεύσεται, from ἔρχομαι, erchomai) with 'in the same manner' (ὃν τρόπον), marks the body as in 'heaven' (οὐρανός, ouranos) and yet to return, which is hard to reconcile with a continuous bodily presence in the elements now.

'I am the true vine' (ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή, with 'I am' from 'to be' = εἰμί, eimi), places the same linking verb 'is' (εἰμί, eimi) between the speaker and a predicate that is plainly not a substantial identity (an identity at the deepest level of being). Alongside 'I am the door' (ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα, John 10:9), 'I am the bread' (ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος, John 6:35, with 'bread' = ἄρτος, artos), 'the rock was Christ' (ἡ πέτρα δὲ ἦν ὁ Χριστός, 1 Corinthians 10:4), and 'these are two covenants' (αὗται γάρ εἰσιν δύο διαθῆκαι, Galatians 4:24, with 'covenants' from διαθήκη, diatheke), this shows the linking verb 'is' (εἰμί, eimi) carrying figurative predication (a 'X is Y' statement used as a figure of speech) where no local presence is meant, which is why the bare 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) in the bread word cannot decide the question.

complicating_texts.resolution: The linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) in 'this is my body' (τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου, with 'body' = σῶμα, soma) is the chief lexical support a presence reading invokes. It is addressed by the lexicon gloss of 'to be' (εἰμί, eimi) as the verb to be with various uses, by the parallel cup word predicating the cup ('cup' = ποτήριον, poterion) as the covenant ('covenant' = διαθήκη, diatheke) which cannot be flat identity, and by the figurative linking verb 'is' (εἰμί, eimi) in 'I am the vine', 'I am the door', 'I am the bread' ('bread' = ἄρτος, artos), 'the rock was Christ', and 'these are two covenants'. The verb is therefore neutral on bodily presence and the verdict is left disputed rather than affirmed on its strength.

'Sharing' or 'participation' (κοινωνία, koinonia) of the body ('body' = σῶμα, soma) and blood is the genuine real-presence-flavored anchor that consubstantiation (the teaching that Christ's body is present alongside the bread) shares with the substantial-change ('substantial' meaning at the deepest level of being) and spiritual-presence readings. It is addressed by noting that 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) is glossed participation and across its occurrences means fellowship and sharing, so it affirms a real participation in Christ without specifying that the participation is by a bodily presence in or under the bread as opposed to a spiritual or covenantal union. It underdetermines the proposition.

'Gnaw' or 'chew' (τρώγω, trogo), to gnaw or chew, is the strongest single word on the realism side and is weighed honestly as such. It is addressed by observing that the visceral verb forces the realism of true participation in Christ but does not itself supply the metaphysics (the deep account of what is really going on at the level of being) of how the 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) is present, and by John 6:63 in the same discourse saying the flesh ('flesh' = σάρξ, sarx) profits nothing and the words are spirit, so it does not establish a bodily presence in or under bread.

'Until he comes' (ἄχρι οὗ ἔλθῃ, with 'until' = ἄχρι, achri, and 'come' = ἔρχομαι, erchomai), frames the rite as a proclamation during the Lord's awaited absence. This complicates the affirmation by presupposing he is not yet bodily come, and it is weighed as evidence against a continuous bodily presence in the element, contributing to the disputed verdict.

'Flesh and bones' (σάρξ καὶ ὀστέα, with 'flesh' = σάρξ, sarx) with 'touch' or 'handle' (ψηλαφάω, pselaphao) describes a locally bounded, touchable risen body. This complicates a body that would be bodily present with bread in many places simultaneously. It is addressed by treating the localized character of the risen body as a genuine tension that keeps the verdict disputed rather than affirmed, while not by itself foreclosing accounts that allow a multiplied or spiritual mode of presence.

'The flesh profits nothing' (ἡ σὰρξ οὐκ ὠφελεῖ οὐδέν, with 'flesh' = σάρξ, sarx) is not fully resolvable on lexical grounds alone, because whether 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) here denies a fleshly eating of the bread or names a broader carnal mode of understanding is itself contested. The referent of 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) in this one verse cannot be settled from morphology and concordance data in the bundle, so it is left open and flagged.

variants.note: The bundle reports no variant units (places where manuscripts disagree on the wording) for the cited verses and marks the passages outside current ECM apparatus scope (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants), so the CBGM apparatus (a specific manuscript-comparison tool) was treated as shadow. The minor textual marks at 1 Corinthians 11:24 and 11:25, such as the optional clause about the body given for you, do not alter the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin, from εἰμί, eimi), the 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) wording in 1 Corinthians 10:16, or the remembrance frame on which the verdict turns.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin, from εἰμί, eimi) as a real predication so that the body and blood are present in, with, and under the bread and wine while the elements remain bread and wine. Its strongest lexical support is 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) in 1 Corinthians 10:16, a real participation in the body and blood, and 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo) in John 6, a visceral eating, together with the unqualified linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin). The reading is genuinely available, but the 'in, with, and under' specification (a precise philosophical claim about location) is not in the vocabulary, and 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) means participation without naming a bodily mode, so the support is real yet not decisive.

Takes the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin, from εἰμί, eimi) as a strict identity in which the bread becomes the body so that what remains is the body under the appearance of bread. It shares the 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) and 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo) anchors with the consubstantiation reading (bodily-present-alongside reading) and presses the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) toward identity. The vocabulary does not distinguish a change of substance (a change at the deepest level of being) from a presence alongside the substance, so the words cannot adjudicate between this reading and consubstantiation, and both face the figurative-linking-verb counterweight.

Reads 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) as a true spiritual participation in Christ received by faith, and John 6:63, 'the Spirit gives life, the flesh ('flesh' = σάρξ, sarx) profits nothing,' as steering reception toward a spiritual mode rather than a local bodily one. This is well supported by the participation vocabulary and by the John 6 discourse, but the contested referent of 'flesh' (σάρξ, sarx) in John 6:63 keeps it from being confirmed on lexical data alone.

Leans on 'for my remembrance' (εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν, with 'remembrance' = ἀνάμνησις, anamnesis), repeated twice, on the figurative linking verb 'is' (εἰμί, eimi) in 'I am the vine' and 'I am the door', and on 'until he comes' (ἄχρι οὗ ἔλθῃ, with 'until' = ἄχρι, achri, and 'come' = ἔρχομαι, erchomai), to read the rite as remembrance and proclamation during bodily absence. This is strongly supported by the surrounding lexis (vocabulary), but it does not erase the literal availability of the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin) or the force of 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) and 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo), so it too falls short of closing the question lexically.

hermeneutics.notes: By analogy of Scripture the cup word, the 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) of 1 Corinthians 10:16, the 'gnaw' (τρώγω, trogo) discourse and its John 6:63 qualifier, and the ascension and resurrection narratives are read alongside the bread word. The linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin, from εἰμί, eimi) remains the pivot, and because 'to be' (εἰμί, eimi) is two-valued in usage and 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia) names participation without specifying a bodily mode, no single lens resolves the proposition on lexis (vocabulary) and morphology (word-form analysis) alone.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: How should the words 'this is my body' and 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' be understood in relation to the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, and what does the canon indicate about the mode and the location of Christ's body in that rite?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem encodes a specific metaphysical formula (a precise philosophical claim about how something exists), bodily present in, with, and under the elements without the elements being substantially changed (changed at the deepest level of being), which presupposes a particular construal of the linking verb 'is' (ἐστιν, estin, from εἰμί, eimi), of 'sharing' (κοινωνία, koinonia), and a particular christological account of the body. The verdict is derived on the original stem from lexical evidence regardless of which tradition the formula favors. The neutralized form removes the preloaded metaphysical claim and asks the open lexical question about mode and location.

lay_summary: This proposition says Christ is bodily present in, with, and under the bread and wine while the bread and wine stay bread and wine. The lexical pivot is the little linking verb 'is' (estin, from the Greek verb 'to be' eimi) in the words 'this is my body' in 1 Corinthians 11:24. The Greek verb 'is' (estin), which the lexicon describes as the verb to be with various uses, is used in the New Testament both for plain identity and for figurative predication (a 'X is Y' statement used as a figure of speech), so the grammar by itself does not force a bodily presence in the element. The parallel cup saying shows this, because it says 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood', and the cup is plainly not the covenant in a flat literal sense, and the same linking verb carries figures in 'I am the vine', 'I am the door', 'I am the bread', 'the rock was Christ', and 'these are two covenants'. There is real weight on the presence side. In 1 Corinthians 10:16 Paul calls the cup a sharing in the blood of Christ and the bread a sharing in the body of Christ, using the word 'sharing' (koinonia), and in John 6 Jesus uses a strong word, 'gnaw' or 'chew' (trogo), for eating his flesh. But 'sharing' (koinonia) means participation or fellowship, and it does not say whether that participation comes by a body located in or under the bread, by a change of substance, by a spiritual receiving, or by covenant union. The words leave the how unspecified. Other texts pull the other way. The phrase 'for my remembrance' appears twice, and Paul says the church proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, which assumes the Lord is awaited and not yet bodily arrived. In Acts the same body is lifted up and taken into heaven and is said to return in the same way it left. In Luke the risen Jesus is handled and shows flesh ('flesh' is sarx in Greek) and bones in one place. And in John the saying 'the flesh profits nothing and the words are spirit' steers the eating toward a spiritual mode. The honest reading of the word data is that this is materially contested. The linking verb can bear a presence reading and 'sharing' (koinonia) and 'gnaw' (trogo) give it real footing, but the 'in, with, and under' specification is a metaphysical claim the vocabulary never makes, so the lexical evidence by itself neither affirms nor denies the formula.
